creator: Elephants in Rooms - Ken LaCorte
title: ISIS was the biggest story on Earth ... then it vanished
full_text:
Whatever happened to ISIS? Think back
about 10 years. For a while, ISIS was
the biggest story on Earth. A brand new
terrorist state carved out of a rock in
Syria. They grew quickly and soon had
millions of people under their control,
and they were absolutely horrific. They
kept showing off more and more creative
ways that they could kill their enemies,
and then they'd publish them with slick
music videos. It was like the Nazis took
over MTV. We were told they might last
for generations. And then almost
overnight, they seemed to disappear. So,
what happened? I'm Ken LeCourt, and
today's elephant in the room is that the
most theatrically evil organization of
our lifetimes disappeared so quickly
that most people don't even know the
story. I didn't until I researched this.
And that story is a messy, expensive one
in both money and bloodshed all around.
Here's the road map. First, the terror
show, what these guys actually were.
Then, what they wanted, the ideology.
After that, we'll look at how they were
beaten, as well as the price of winning.
And finally, where it went, because a
thing like that doesn't completely
disappear. So, let's talk about the
terror show. If you were online between
2014 and 2017, you probably saw snippets
of their videos whether you wanted to or
not. I remember some of them as clear as
yesterday. In one, a Jordanian pilot had
been captured after his plane went down
over Syria. ISIS locked him in a cage,
doused him with gasoline, and burned him
alive. They filmed it from multiple
angles with a music score, like a movie.
In another video, 21 Coptic Christians
in orange jumpsuits were marched onto a
Libyan beach and beheaded. In another,
prisoners were lined up along the
Euphrates and executed like it was an
assembly line. At a place called Sinjar
in northern Iraq, they came for the
Yazidis, a small religious minority ISIS
decided to wipe out. Men and boys were
shot and buried in pits. Women and girls
were sorted by age and and sold as sex
slaves. There were actual price lists.
That's the horror, and the scale of it
was massive. I mean, we don't really
have an accurate body count, but it's
safe to say that they killed tens of
thousands of civilians during their run.
At its peak in 2015, ISIS controlled the
lives of roughly 8 million people under
its rule. Its footprint was about 35,000
square miles, an area about the size of
Portugal spread across Iraq and Syria.
And they ran it like a government. They
collected taxes and ran the police,
courts, and schools. They handled
mundane things like birth certificates
and marriage licenses.
It was also, by a wide margin, the
richest terror operation in history. The
RAND Corporation says that it made
nearly a half billion dollars just from
oil in just 1 year.
ISIS also taxed those 8 million people,
looted banks, and ran extortion rackets
on everything that moved. But the land
and the money, that wasn't the
innovation. What made ISIS really
different was the media machine that
produced those videos.
Propaganda wasn't just a side project
for them. At their peak, a single month
saw over a thousand separate pieces of
propaganda, videos, photo essays,
magazine articles, and radio bulletins.
And most of it wasn't gore. More than
half was lifestyle stuff, like markets
full of food, kids in classrooms, happy
footage of a paradise caliphate. The
beheading videos got the clicks, but the
travel brochure videos, that's what
closed the sale. And it worked. The
pitch, come help help build a state,
watch us burn our enemies alive? That
lured over 40,000 foreigners from over
110 countries. People left their
comfortable lives in London, Paris,
Minneapolis, and flew across the world
to join them. Several hundred came from
the United States alone. Why did they do
that? You know, it reminded me of an
interview I read shortly after 9/11 with
a man living in Afghanistan. And when he
was asked what he wanted to do with his
life, he said he either wanted to join
the jihad against the United States or
move to New York City and become a taxi
driver. Now, on the face of that, it it
it seemed pretty opposite. It seems
ridiculous. But when you think about it,
he was really saying he wanted a bigger
life attached to something special. And
those are the paths to a bigger life
that he saw. All right. In just a
minute, I'll tell you what ISIS promised
guys like that who followed the first
path.

Okay, so back to the crazy story of
ISIS. One thing to note is that they had
a plan. The terror had a goal and a
twisted logic to it. So, let's take a
look at what they wanted, starting with
their ideology. In their reading of
Islam, a caliphate is a religious
obligation. That's a single Islamic
state ruled by a single successor to the
prophet. And on the 4th of July, 2014, a
man named Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi walked
into the Great Mosque of al-Nuri in
Mosul. He had flowing black robes and
declared himself that successor, the
leader of all Muslims everywhere. Now,
most of the world's 1.8 billion Muslims
looked at this guy and said, "No,
thanks." But, he planted his flag. And
there's a theological twist that
mattered later. According to a prophecy,
the farm town of Dabiq in northern Syria
was where the army of Islam would meet
the armies of the West for one of the
final battles before the end of the
world. They cared about this town so
much that they named their glossy
English language magazine after it. This
is why holding physical land mattered so
much to them, in a way it never did for
al-Qaeda. ISIS claimed to be the
fulfillment of a prophecy, which is a
great recruiting pitch, especially when
you're winning. But, it's a serious
problem when you start losing because if
God promised you this land and you lose
it, what does that say about you? What
does it say about the promise? ISIS also
went to war with history itself. On
camera, they took sledgehammers and
power tools to priceless statues in the
Mosul Museum. They blew up ancient
temples in Palmyra, the 2,000-year-old
ruins in Syria. Their logic was simple.
Anything that existed before their
version of Islam had no right to exist
at all. Erase the past and you get to
pretend that you're the beginning of the
world. And ISIS wanted to fight
everyone. They declared war on Shia-led
governments in Iraq and Iran, on Sunni
monarchies like Saudi Arabia, on the
West, on the Kurds. ISIS was so out of
control that Al-Qaeda formally cut ties
with them in 2014,
and then they went to war with each
other. So, literally, the United States
and the West was fighting on the same
side as Al-Qaeda. By the way, if I make
any substantive mistake here, I'll
address it in a pinned comment below.
Look, this is a topic where the sourcing
gets contested and the numbers get
fought over, so have at it. So, the
world has this awful thing. How do you
destroy it? Here's the story of how they
were beaten. First, the setup. The war
against ISIS ran across two presidents
who agreed on almost nothing. Barack
Obama and Donald Trump. And to this day,
supporters of each will tell you that
their guy is the one who really won.
I'll walk you through what happened as
straight as I can and let you decide.
Start with the slow years. In January
2014, ISIS rolled into Fallujah, an
Iraqi city where a lot of Americans had
bled a decade earlier. That same month,
President Obama diminished the group to
a reporter with a basketball metaphor,
saying, "If a JV team puts on Lakers
jerseys, that doesn't make them Kobe
Bryant." It was a good line, and it aged
very poorly.
13 months later, his tone had changed
completely. Obama was calling ISIS a
generational struggle, and the working
assumption in Washington was that this
could be a war that lasted a decade or
more. Obama's strategy had a name,
Operation Inherent Resolve. And the core
idea was no big American ground
presence. The military called it by,
with, and through.
This meant American and coalition war
planes would own the sky. American
special forces would advise and train,
but the actual walking into the bullets
would be done by local forces, the Iraqi
army.
And in Syria, a Kurdish and Arab militia
called the Syrian Democratic Forces, the
SDF.
The people doing the dying on the ground
were overwhelmingly Iraqi and Kurdish.
The SDF alone lost something like 11,000
fighters. The buy with through approach
worked, but slowly. Still, about half of
ISIS fighters were killed during the
Obama years, and by the time he left
office in January 2017,
the coalition had clawed back roughly
half of ISIS's territory. Now, here's
where we have to be careful because both
sides kind of cherry-pick this number.
That half that got retaken under Obama
was mostly the easier half, open
countryside and smaller towns. The two
hardest targets, the two big cities of
Mosul in Iraq and Raqqa in Syria, those
were brutal urban fights, and those got
finished under Trump. So, for most of
the campaign against ISIS, a lot of US
commanders chafed at the Obama
administration's sensitivity to the
number of US boots on the ground and
restrictive rules of engagement that
required White House approval for many
lethal strikes. Now, that began to
loosen in literally the last weeks of
the Obama administration,
and then Trump's Pentagon pushed it
further and faster.
What actually changed when the
administrations flipped? Primarily two
things. First, the safety came off the
trigger. Under the new team, Defense
Secretary James Mattis and the field
commanders, they got more authority to
approve strikes on their own without
every decision having to be routed back
to Washington, D.C. Now, when a
commander in the field can destroy
targets in minutes instead of waiting
days, perhaps for a sign-off, the pace
of war changes. Second, the goal itself
changed. Mattis described the shift
bluntly, from attrition to annihilation.
The old way was to push ISIS out of a
city and let the survivors run to fight
another day. The new way was to surround
a city first, seal the exits, and
destroy every fighter where they stood,
no escape quarter. And in May 2017,
Trump approved shipping heavy weapons
directly to the Syrian Kurds for the
assault on Raqqa. Turkey, a NATO ally
that considers those same Kurds to be
terrorists, they were furious. Obama had
refused to do it for exactly that
reason. Trump did it anyway, but that
also came with a later twist. Then came
the collapse, and it was ugly as war
gets. The battle for Mosul, it ground on
for 9 months, block by block, house by
house. It was the biggest urban battle
any army had fought in since World War
II. Raqqa was even more intense. One
single Marine artillery battalion in 5
months fired 35,000 rounds into the
city. To put that in perspective, the
entire American invasion of Iraq back in
2003 used slightly fewer rounds. The end
came in March 2019 in a filthy tent camp
on a river near a village called
Baghouz. The caliphate that had once
ruled 8 million people ended with a few
hundred cornered fighters in the mud.
So, the caliphate was gone. Now, let's
look at the price of winning. But, look,
let me say plainly because it matters.
The people who planned it, the people
who fought it and pulled it off, they
did something genuinely hard and
worthwhile. But, nobody back home ever
seemed to add up those costs. By the end
of 2016, the Pentagon had already spent
close to $11 billion on the anti-ISIS
campaign. And that clock kept running
for 3 more years. The final tab, it ran
deep into the tens of billions of
dollars for a war a lot of Americans
barely remember. But, also, let's look
at what annihilation actually looked
like on the ground. Think of that one
Marine battalion at Raqqa, and now the
same amount of firepower coming from a
whole coalition pounding one city for
months on end. When the smoke cleared,
about 80% of Raqqa was uninhabitable. I
mean, most of that destruction wasn't
ISIS. There were 10,000 destroyed
buildings. And that was overwhelmingly
our bombs and our shells. We had to
destroy Raqqa to save it, as the saying
goes.
There's also a fight over how many
civilians died. So, let me give you both
sides of that. Amnesty International
says that more than 1,600 civilians were
killed by coalition strikes in Raqqa.
The coalition said 159 at first, then
later raised that figure to 318. So,
that's not a small gap. Who's right?
Well, Amnesty sent teams to Raqqa and
combed through millions of frames of
satellite imagery. Their number has fair
critics. In an urban firefight, it's
hard to know whether a death came from a
coalition shell or an ISIS mortar, and
ISIS deliberately used civilians as
human shields. But, the coalition's
figures, they probably have a bigger
problem. They mostly reviewed their own
strike logs and kind of waved away
outside reports as non-credible. There
were two other bills that came due after
the shooting stopped. The first came in
October 2019. With ISIS beaten,
President Trump got on the phone with
Turkey's president, and days later, he
pulled American troops back from
northeastern Syria. Then, Turkey
immediately invaded, going after the
SDF. Those are the coalition's Kurdish
allies who just lost 11,000 of their own
people fighting ISIS. So, overnight,
America's battlefield partner was left
exposed to a NATO army that considered
them terrorists. More than 200,000
people fled, and the outrage in
Washington was really bipartisan, and
some of the loudest critics were Trump's
fellow Republicans who called it
abandoning an ally. The second lingering
bill is still sitting out in the desert.
Because, when the caliphate fell, it
left behind tens of thousands of ISIS
fighters and their families with nowhere
to go. They ended up in a a sprawling
detention camps in Kurdish-held Syria.
The biggest one swelled to nearly 74,000
people at one point, most of them women
and children, 60% under the age of 18.
And, as is often the case, no one wanted
them. Country after country refused to
take back their own citizens because
repatriating suspected terrorists, it's
a political grenade that no politician
wants to be left holding. The danger in
that isn't hypothetical. In January
2022, ISIS remnants launched a massive
assault on a prison that was holding
thousands of its fighters. To stop it
took days of fighting and American help.
Hundreds died. Analysts started using a
chilling phrase. They called the camp an
ISIS university. A place where a whole
new generation of kids is marinating in
that ideology, waiting. Okay, so where
ISIS went is a real question because a
state the size of Portugal doesn't just
evaporate. And where it went is a
strange story. Start with the
leadership. Seven months after losing
the last of the caliphate in October
2019, American special forces cornered
al-Baghdadi, the man who declared
himself the caliph in that Mosul mosque.
They had him pinned in a tunnel in
northwestern Syria. He blew himself up
with a suicide vest, killing two of his
own children with him. Then, his
successor, a guy called al-Qurashi, died
in a US raid in February 2022. He also
blew himself up. The next leader was
killed later that same year. The one
after that, a year later. The current
guy took over in 2023 and almost nobody
knows who he actually is. He's never
released an image or an audio message.
The self-proclaimed leader of all
Muslims on Earth is now a man whose own
name is a mystery. So, first the good
news. The caliphate is actually gone. No
territory, no oil fields, tens of
thousands of their fighters, they're
dead. The new rulers of Syria, they hunt
ISIS instead of tolerating it. Attacks
inside of Iraq and Syria, they've fallen
to historic lows. By the numbers, ISIS
is weaker in its old stomping ground
than at any point since it first showed
up in 2013. That was a genuine military
defeat and in that place, it's not
coming back. But, here's where the
script takes a bit of a twist. While
everyone was watching the caliphate die
in the Middle East, ISIS quietly became
something it had never been before, a
franchise. ISIS Central built real
corporate bureaucracies to manage its
branches around the world. Regional
offices with actual names, budgets, and
reporting lines. The most important one
at the moment is in the mountains of
Somalia, a country most people don't
associate with ISIS. That branch is now
the group's ATM.
It shakes down businesses and moves
money across the continent. It pulls in
over $4 million a year and some of that
cash it gets wired out to other branches
via crypto. ISIS is nowhere near its
past strength, but it's causing
terrorism still. Now, most of the
jihadist violence happening across
Africa right now, it's really local even
though sometimes they call themselves
ISIS. But, there's a connected core,
including the one in Afghanistan, called
ISIS-K. They're the ones who bombed the
Abbey Gate Kabul Airport during the
chaotic American withdrawal from
Afghanistan. That attack killed 13 US
service members and about 170 Afghan
civilians. In Moscow in 2024, they shot
up a concert hall killing nearly 150
people and injuring hundreds more. It
was the deadliest terror attack in
Russia in decades and the US
intelligence community had actually
warned Moscow it was coming. And when
President Assad's brutal regime finally
collapsed in Syria, the group that
ousted him was led by a former jihadist
who's now president of Syria. But, he
wasn't an ISIS jihadist and he expelled
the remnants of them from Syria. So, for
a decade everyone assumed that the
minute America left, ISIS would come
roaring back and that really just hasn't
happened in its own home. There, the
caliphate it just doesn't exist. So,
that's the answer to where it went. The
state is dead, but the ideology to some
extent went portable, out to Somalia and
Afghanistan and Nigeria, and undoubtedly
the terrorists whose names we don't know
yet. Some of the remnants are still
around, but ISIS as we know it is gone.
Definitely for now,
hopefully for good. You know, going
through this piece, it's easy to see why
growing numbers of American say, "Enough
with that whole region. It's too bloody,
too expensive, and we have enough
troubles at home, and they they keep
switching sides." I mean, from my point
of view, it makes me want to see
everyone move away from fossil fuels
because even if the United States drills
all the oil it needs, the world oil

and it's so much centered on that
region. I mean, it really makes me root
for solar, nuclear, anything else that
wouldn't drag the world into that region
so often. Or, is it all about Israel? Do
Jewish Americans and Israelis in effect
control the foreign policy of the United
States? A lot more people are saying
that these days, so I dug into answering
that question fairly. YouTube didn't
seem to like that video, but you might.
It's linked in the description if it
doesn't show up here. Hey, thanks for
watching. I gave this to you as straight
as I could, and I hope you found it
worthy of your time. I take that
seriously.
See you again.

notes.note: ISIS lost its last territorial stronghold, Baghuz, Syria, in March 2019 — not October 2019. Al-Baghdadi was killed by U.S. special forces in October 2019, about seven months after Baghuz fell, not seven months after an October 2019 loss.
notes.claim: Al-Baghdadi was cornered by American special forces seven months after ISIS lost the last of its caliphate territory.

sources.quote: On March 23, 2019, almost exactly five years ago, the Coalition and its local partners liberated the final stretch of territory controlled by ISIS in Baghuz, Syria.
sources.explanation: Confirms that the final territorial stronghold of ISIS was lost in March 2019, not October 2019.

sources.quote: On October 26–27, 2019, the United States conducted a military operation codenamed Operation Kayla Mueller that resulted in the death of Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi
sources.explanation: Confirms Baghdadi was killed in October 2019.
